_comment: A feature is what a project asks for; a template is what kibo renders. This file is the
map between them, so templates stay flat and selection is expressed one level up.
`requires` was measured, not decided: it is the #include graph of the generated C++,
interface (.hpp -> .hpp) and build (.cpp -> .hpp) unioned, since asking for a feature
means compiling it. Re-measure it when the templates move.

Base.doc: The type system and everything that cannot be pulled apart from it. Data, Codec, Model and AnyConcept include one another in both directions; there is no cut.

Fields.doc: Field addressing. Depends on nothing and nothing depends on it but Attachments.

Database.doc: The operations a stored attachment gains.

Attachments.note: Database is in `requires` because Attachments.cpp includes Db.hpp -- measured, not intended. The dependency runs backwards: a database adds operations to attachments, so a project that wants attachments and no database cannot have them. The edge is a template defect, not a fact about the model.

AttachmentPool.doc: The model's attachments exposed to the dynamic world.

Pool.doc: A function pool. Still holds its own remote side -- see cpp/README.md.

Test.doc: What it takes to put a unit to the test.

TestApp.doc: The programme that runs the test over the whole model.

Base.doc: The package: its entry point, the types each namespace declares, the attachments, and the container bindings the model mentions.

Pool.doc: A function pool and its client edge. Most projects have none: a pool is a service surface, not a consequence of having a model.
Pool.note: Selecting Base alone leaves out pool.py.stg, but not the pool's own entry point: __init__.py.stg declares the `pool` entry itself, so kibo still renders a package directory for every pool. Expressing "no pools" fully means moving that entry out of __init__.py.stg, not choosing differently here. Measured, not assumed.

Wheel.doc: What makes the package installable, and therefore typed.
Wheel.note: These two do not land beside the modules: py.typed goes inside the package, pyproject.toml one level up at the project root. A project script renders them with a different -o. Measured: without py.typed a consumer gets `Stub file not found` and every annotation in the package is invisible; without pyproject.toml `pip install` refuses the directory outright.
